cls: Local anesthetic - topical (non-amide, non-ester surface anesthetic)
quick: Apply 1% cream/lotion/gel to affected area up to 3-4 times daily
Limited data; topical absorption low - use if needed
Limited data; minimal systemic exposure expected
summary: Pramoxine is a surface local anesthetic that is chemically distinct from the amide and ester classes, making cross-sensitivity uncommon. It is used topically to relieve pain and itching from minor skin conditions, insect bites, hemorrhoids, and minor burns. Onset is rapid and effect is local; systemic absorption through intact skin is minimal.
indications: Temporary relief of pain and itching associated with minor cuts, scrapes, minor burns, sunburn and insect bites
Relief of itching and discomfort from hemorrhoids and anorectal irritation
Temporary relief of itching due to minor skin irritations and rashes

dosage.d: Apply 1% product externally to anal area
dosage.n: After bowel movements and as needed

dosage.d: Apply thin film to affected area

admin: For external use only; apply to clean, dry skin
Avoid contact with eyes; do not apply to large denuded or severely traumatized areas
Do not apply to deep or puncture wounds or use over extensive surfaces
Wash hands after application unless treating the hands
Discontinue and consult a clinician if condition worsens or persists beyond 7 days
moa: Pramoxine stabilizes the neuronal membrane and decreases its permeability to sodium ions, blocking initiation and conduction of nerve impulses and thereby producing local surface anesthesia and relief of pain and itch at the application site.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to pramoxine or any formulation component
relative: Broken, severely inflamed or infected skin (increased absorption)
Application to eyes or mucous membranes not labeled for such use

preg: Limited data in pregnancy. Systemic absorption from topical use is low; use only if clearly needed.
lact: Limited data during breastfeeding. Minimal systemic exposure is expected; avoid application to the nipple/areola where the infant could ingest it.
renal: No dosage adjustment needed for topical use given minimal systemic absorption.
hepatic: No dosage adjustment needed for topical use given minimal systemic absorption.

minor: Other topical agents on the same site may alter absorption or cause local irritation

common: Transient burning or stinging at application site
emergency: Anaphylaxis (rare, with extensive or mucosal application)

monitoring: Local skin response and signs of sensitization
Resolution of symptoms; reassess if not improved within about 7 days
counsel: For external use only - keep away from the eyes
A brief stinging or burning sensation may occur after application
Do not use on deep wounds, serious burns or large raw areas
Stop use and seek advice if redness, swelling or irritation worsens
Do not use longer than directed without consulting a clinician
pk: Maximal local effect shortly after onset
Not well characterized; systemic absorption minimal
Local anesthesia lasts up to several hours
Store at room temperature; keep from freezing; protect from heat
pearls: Chemically unrelated to amide (e.g., lidocaine) and ester (e.g., benzocaine) anesthetics, so cross-sensitivity is uncommon
Frequently combined with hydrocortisone for anorectal and pruritic skin products
Unlike benzocaine, it carries little to no risk of methemoglobinemia at usual topical doses
Effect is purely local; not used for injectable or infiltration anesthesia
missed: As an as-needed topical product, simply apply when symptoms occur; there is no fixed dose to make up. Do not exceed the labeled frequency.
overdose: Topical overdose is unlikely. Excessive application to broken skin or mucosa could theoretically cause systemic local-anesthetic toxicity (CNS excitation/depression, cardiovascular effects); manage with supportive care and remove the product.
